quote: it would be rare to find a city merchant who believed the sky was blue, and yet advocated an individual tax and freer marriage laws
content: The fable stipulates that partisans genuinely anticipate different sky colors, and the six endings depend on it. Real partisan "factual" disagreement is substantially expressive: paying respondents for accurate answers cut the partisan gap on factual questions roughly in half (Bullock et al. 2015; Prior, Sood & Khanna 2015), and mass polarization is on affect toward the other side rather than on issue positions (Iyengar, Sood & Lelkes 2012). By the standard of this sequence's own later essays (Belief as Attire), the likelier Underground is one in which almost nobody anticipates anything about the sky and "cerulean is green" is a cheer. In that world the reveal changes nothing, and the fable has no story.

quote: Now history branches, depending on which member of the sightseeing party decided to follow the corridor to the surface.
content: What happens when partisans meet decisive contrary evidence has been measured. The "backfire effect" dramatized by Aditya and Barron, in which correction strengthens the false belief, was reported once (Nyhan & Reifler 2010) and then failed to replicate across more than 10,000 subjects and 52 issues: people update the fact (Wood & Porter 2019). But updated facts leave candidate evaluations and policy attitudes essentially untouched (Nyhan, Porter, Reifler & Wood 2020). The realistic seventh ending is that the Underground accepts the sky is blue within a week and the tax and marriage disputes continue unchanged. The fable's load-bearing premise, that one factual question holds up an entire political coalition, is the part with the least support.

quote: Ferris gasped involuntarily, frozen by sheer wonder and delight.
content: Ferris is the only character with no faction, no family, no colleagues and no stake, and the only one framed as admirable. The fable thus equates rationality with having nothing to lose, which is a fact about Ferris's situation, not Ferris's cognition. Daria, who pays the real cost of updating, is portrayed as mournful rather than exemplary. Partisan identity functions as a social identity whose costs are what actually block updating (Iyengar et al. 2012; Mason 2018, Uncivil Agreement, book, no DOI), so the fable's chosen hero is precisely the person for whom that mechanism is switched off. A parable that demonstrates its thesis by exempting its hero from the thesis's difficulty has demonstrated nothing.

By the standard of the preceding essay this one pays no rent: six invented characters constrain no anticipation, and Yudkowsky elsewhere warns explicitly against generalizing from fictional evidence. Fictional evidence about human psychology written by the person arguing for the conclusion does whatever the argument needs. The one historical datum is accurate as far as it goes, but the standard modern study of the Byzantine factions (Cameron 1976, Circus Factions, book, no DOI) finds they also brokered patronage and employment, and in the Nika riots of 532 Blues and Greens united against Justinian over taxes and hated officials. Even the essay's own case of "pure" arbitrary-marker hostility had material interests under the colors.
